summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is criminalised under section 377 of the Penal Code of 1861, a provision introduced in 1886. It prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman or animal and provides for imprisonment ranging between life and a term of not less than two years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of between 400 and 1,000 rupees. The prohibition applies regardless of consent or privacy, and it reaches heterosexual anal and oral sex as well. Enforcement has been described as inconsistent, but the provision remains in active use: in November 2018 the HIV-positive advocate Aung Myo Htut, also known as Addy Chen, was charged under it in Yangon over an alleged offence against an employee. A June 2024 submission by Human Rights Myanmar to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions reports that section 377 enforcement has intensified since the coup of 1 February 2021 and operates as an aggravating factor in proceedings against LGBTIQ+ people.

Transgender people are additionally targeted under section 35(c) of the Police Act 1945, known locally as the shadow law or darkness law, which allows police to detain anyone they consider to be behaving suspiciously after sunset. A March 2025 report states that this provision is applied specifically against transgender people and that it carries up to three months' detention for face covering. Other provisions cited as usable against LGBTQ people include sections 269 and 270 on negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease, section 290 on public nuisance with fines up to 200 rupees, sections 292, 293 and 294 on obscene material, songs or public acts, section 372, section 469 on a marriage ceremony absent a legal marriage, and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act on anything affecting morality negatively.

Myanmar does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, and the state does not recognise their gender identity. No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for trans people is documented in the sources.

Police violence against transgender women is recorded in specific cases. In 2016 a trans woman in Yangon described arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days of detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work. In 2013 police in Mandalay arrested trans women and forced them to strip and parade naked while being photographed, an action police described as a public service. The sources also record police harassment, sexual assault including rape, mistreatment and extortion directed at transgender people.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021, post-coup authorities have committed attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people, according to a January 2024 report. The parallel government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured from 1 February 2021 to the report date, while Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission gives a figure of 5 to 12 individuals dead in military-controlled Myanmar since the coup. Both figures are raw counts without a denominator, and the sources provide no general homicide rate for the same period against which they can be set.

Outright International's overview, updated March 2026, reports that section 377 is used to detain people who cannot satisfactorily account for their presence, and that risks intensified after the coup: torture and sexual violence in detention, an October 2022 organisation registration law carrying prison terms for NGO non-compliance, compulsory military service announced in February 2024, and seven LGBTQ-themed books banned in 2025. Its assessment is to avoid the country entirely.

The 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement, according to a March 2025 report drawing on community research conducted in January 2025. In January 2025 the authorities banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions for their publishers.

A survey of LGBT respondents reported in January 2024 found that 50% had no confidence in the legal system and more than 68% feared repercussions from abusers.

Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. The 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals but carry no legal penalties, and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery while remaining a planning document rather than an enforceable law.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Cohabitation and ceremonial marriages carry no legal standing; a 2014 unofficial wedding by a same-sex couple together for ten years triggered a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them.

Access to healthcare is shaped by criminalisation and stigma. Section 377 was called out in 2013 as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men living with HIV/AIDS face particular stigma.
tangentialFactors:
A 2020 poll found that 74% of respondents agreed that being LGBTQ should be legal, with 23% disagreeing, and 81% agreed that LGBTQ people deserve equality and equal treatment, with 12% disagreeing. LGBTQ activists have described a growing climate of societal acceptance in line with wider international trends. These figures measure general public opinion rather than the treatment a trans visitor would receive, and the poll's field period closed before the 2021 coup.

Social mores around sexuality are described as extremely conservative, and in local Buddhist tradition those born LGBTQ are perceived as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life. Historically, official homophobia, limited public awareness and a lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in Burmese society.

Transgender women who work as nat kadaws, or spirit mediums, can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them, and the term Occult is described as a local name for the transgender community. Visibility of this kind coexists with criminalisation: trans women are frequently denied equal access to professions, and the sources describe beautician, fashion designer and nat kadaw as the only careers considered respectable for them, which contributes to overrepresentation in spirit medium work and sex work.

In June 2019 a young gay librarian, Kyaw Zin Win, died by suicide at a university in Yangon after sustained harassment and bullying from colleagues. More than 600 people attended his funeral, the university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for anti-discrimination provisions to be enacted. The case concerned a gay man rather than a trans person, but it evidences the absence of enforceable workplace protection.

A statement attributed to a lesbian woman from Myanmar holds that lesbians are often seen as less acceptable than gay men and transgender people, indicating that hostility within the wider community is not evenly distributed.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents have no route to legal recognition: the gender assigned at birth cannot be changed, so official documents continue to carry a marker that does not match their presentation, and every interaction requiring an identity document risks exposure. Police use section 35(c) of the Police Act 1945 against transgender people specifically, most readily after sunset, and the documented pattern of arrest includes stripping, beating, forced photography and extortion.

Employment discrimination narrows the work available to trans women to a small set of accepted roles, with spirit medium work and sex work the outcomes for many, and sex work in turn exposes them to the criminal law. Family rejection and violence for gender identity are documented experiences of transgender people.

Resident civil society operates under the October 2022 organisation registration law, which carries prison terms for non-compliance, and the 2024 Conscription Law has produced fear and displacement among queer residents. Compulsory military service was announced in February 2024.

The protections that exist are symbolic. The 2019 Child Rights Law clause covers sexual orientation only for children and has no enforcement mechanism, the 2020 broadcasting guidelines carry no penalties, and the 2022 gender policy is a planning document. There is no enforceable anti-discrimination law for adults on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions.

HIV services are affected by section 377 and by stigma toward gay men living with HIV/AIDS. The 2022 gender policy names LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, which shapes how services are planned rather than creating an individual right.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address entry, visa or border procedures for trans visitors, and nothing is sourced on document-marker screening, airport pat-downs or secondary screening triggered by binders, packers or gender presentation. Whether a foreign passport carrying an amended gender marker is accepted at entry is not sourced here.

The killing figures of 17 since 1 February 2021 and 5 to 12 since the coup are raw counts with no denominator and no general homicide rate for the same period, so their magnitude relative to background violence in the country cannot be established from these sources. The two figures also come from different collectors and are not reconciled.

The field period of the survey reporting 50% and 68% figures is not stated in the source text, only the January 2024 publication date. The frequency with which section 377 and section 35(c) are actually enforced is not quantified anywhere in the inventory; the most recent individually documented section 377 charge is from November 2018, and the most recent individually documented police violence against a trans woman described in detail is from 2016, with no later individual case sourced.

Whether the text of section 377 or the Police Act has been amended after 2021 is not sourced. Conditions in territory not under military control are not covered, and the inventory does not establish which of the reported harms are attributable to the state as opposed to non-state actors.
